items.prompt: A tampered client POSTs to /api/attempts with an extra "correct": true and "score": 1 next to a wrong answer. What happens to those two fields?
items.answer: Dropped: checkBody copies just the allow-listed fields, and the server re-grades
distractors: checkBody rejects the whole request with a 400, since unknown fields are forbidden
They are stored as the client's claim and later compared against the server grade
The server accepts them as-is, but only when the response kind is self-graded
items.explanation: checkBody builds a fresh object from exactly itemId, response, timeSpent, mode and attempt, so the server re-grades and stores its own verdict. Dropping by construction (copy the allow-listed fields into a new object) means the client can submit an answer but can never claim a result.

items.prompt: Why does it matter that grade() reads no database, clock or window?
items.answer: The same function runs in the browser and on the server, so the two stay in step
distractors: Pure functions are memoized by React, so each item's grade is computed exactly once
It lets the server skip its own re-grade whenever a client verdict is attached
It is required so that grade() can be called inside a single database transaction
items.explanation: Purity lets the same function run unchanged in the browser for instant feedback and on the server for the authoritative re-grade. A grader that read Date.now(), the DB or window could not run in both places. One pure function serves the client, the route and the content checker.

items.prompt: gradeCode() uses options.runTests ?? runTests. What does this single optional parameter achieve?
items.answer: The server injects the node:vm runner while grader.ts keeps zero node: imports
distractors: It lets the grader detect at runtime whether it is running in Node or a browser
It lets learners supply their own test runner alongside their code submission
It makes code grading asynchronous, so the API can stream test results back
items.explanation: Dependency injection at the smallest useful size: one optional parameter with a default keeps the grader pure and portable - grader.ts still bundles for the browser, and tests can pass a fake runner.

items.prompt: A multi-select item has 2 correct options out of 4. A learner ticks all 4. What score does gradeMulti give?
items.answer: 0 - each false positive cancels a hit; the net is floored at zero
distractors: 1 - both correct options were selected, so the item counts as solved
0.5 - hits and misses are averaged evenly across the four options
-0.5 - the net goes negative, so ticking everything is punished
items.explanation: Each wrong pick cancels one right pick and the net never goes negative, so selecting everything is never a winning strategy.

items.prompt: A learner gets an item right on the second try, but the client sends attempt: 1. Why can't the server catch this?
items.answer: The first miss on a retryable item is not posted, so nothing contradicts it
distractors: It can: the route looks up the earlier attempt row and overrides the field
The grader spots second tries from the shape of the response and caps the score
attempt is ignored by the route, so each success earns full credit anyway
items.explanation: attempt === 2 caps the score at 0.5, but only the client knows it was a second try - the server has no record to check the number against. The route's Trust boundary comment names this documented, accepted local-first risk and the fix (post the first miss).

items.prompt: timeSpent is clamped to 0..3600 seconds. How can a forged value still affect scheduling?
items.answer: A tiny time on a correct, previously-seen review earns Easy, pushing it further out
distractors: A huge value overflows the FSRS interval and schedules the card in the past instead
It has no effect: the server measures the time itself and ignores the client value
A negative value is stored as-is by the route and resets the card back to New
items.explanation: Clamping bounds the range but not the meaning: timeSpent < budget * 0.5 with reps > 0 earns Easy. The route comment lists this as a known limit.

items.prompt: In the browser runner, a submission contains while (true) {}. What does the TIME_BUDGET_MS check do?
items.answer: Nothing - the check runs after the call returns, so the tab simply hangs
distractors: It interrupts the loop after the 2-second budget and reports a timeout verdict
The browser's new Function compile step detects and refuses the infinite loop
It throws a TimeoutError from a setTimeout that was scheduled before the call
items.explanation: The budget check only catches slow code that finishes. JavaScript cannot interrupt a synchronous function from the same thread; preempting a runaway loop client-side needs a terminable Worker.

items.prompt: On the server the same infinite loop is graded through vmCompile. Why does it stop there?
items.answer: runInContext gets a timeout, which V8 enforces even partway through the loop
distractors: The route runs grading in a worker thread that is terminated after 2 seconds
Next.js aborts a request handler that runs past its response deadline
The vm context exposes no while keyword, so the code fails to compile there
items.explanation: Each call runs via vm.Script runInContext with a timeout; Node reports ERR_SCRIPT_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT. vm's timeout is enforced by V8 inside synchronous execution, so liveness is restored even though the code shares the server's thread.

items.prompt: A learner's solution calls arr.sort() on its input. Why can't that corrupt later test cases sharing the same array literal?
items.answer: runTests structured-clones each argument with cloneArgs before a call
distractors: Test inputs are frozen with Object.freeze, so the call to sort() throws
Each test case is re-parsed from JSON storage right before it is run
The vm context copies the arguments automatically on every single call
items.explanation: Structured cloning isolates each test's inputs. Only uncloneable values (functions, objects holding functions) pass through as-is.

items.prompt: Why does seed() derive item ids as item-<authored id> instead of generating a UUID per run?
items.answer: So a re-seed upserts the same row and history keeps pointing at it
distractors: Because better-sqlite3 does not support UUID columns as primary keys
Deterministic ids make seeding faster, since no randomness is generated
So that renaming an item id automatically migrates its learner history
items.explanation: The learner's user_cards and attempts keep pointing at the item they were about. The price is that an authored id becomes a permanent public key: a rename is seen as one removal plus one new item, and the new item starts with a fresh card.

items.prompt: The seeder upserts content rows with onConflictDoUpdate. Which strategy does it use for user_track_progress rows, and why?
items.answer: onConflictDoNothing, so a re-seed leaves a learner's level untouched
distractors: onConflictDoUpdate, so edits to level thresholds reach every learner
DELETE then INSERT, so stale progress rows are cleaned up on each run
None: the seeder skips them, and the API creates the rows lazily
items.explanation: The row is created if missing and never overwritten. Content is a cache that may be refreshed freely; user state exists nowhere else, so the seeder only fills gaps in it.

items.prompt: An item disappears from the content files. What does the current seeder do with its database row?
items.answer: It sets is_published = 0 and keeps the row, so history is not cascaded away
distractors: It deletes the row, and ON DELETE CASCADE then cleans up all of the item's attempts
It leaves the row published, so existing cards keep being scheduled as usual
It renames the row's id with a deleted- prefix to free the old id for reuse
items.explanation: attempts and user_cards cascade on delete, so a hard delete would erase the learner's history. Soft delete: unpublished items drop out of sessions and progress totals, and if the id returns the upsert republishes it with its history intact.

items.front: POST /api/attempts re-grades every answer (src/app/api/attempts/route.ts:114-126). Which two client inputs does it still take on faith, and why is that acceptable here?
items.back: attempt (whether this was the second try) and timeSpent (clamped, but a small value can turn Good into Easy). Reps is single-user and local, so a forged value only fools the person sending it; the fix for a multi-user version is to post the first miss and derive attempt server-side.

items.front: What does the node:vm runner in src/lib/executor.server.ts buy, and what does it explicitly not buy (lines 20-24)?
items.back: Liveness: an accidental infinite loop is stopped by a hard timeout instead of freezing the API. Not isolation: vm is not a security boundary, code can reach the host through prototype tricks. Fine for a local app running the learner's own code; remote code execution for any hosted multi-user version.

items.front: How does the generalised migrate() in src/lib/db/seed.ts:194-232 decide what to ALTER, and when does it refuse?
items.back: It builds SCHEMA_DDL in an in-memory database, compares each existing table's PRAGMA table_info with it, and ADDs any missing column with its NOT NULL and default. A missing primary key or NOT NULL column with no default cannot be added in place, so it throws and points at npm run db:reset. Additive only, idempotent, run before the DDL.

items.front: Why does the seeder DELETE an item's item_concepts rows and re-insert them (src/lib/db/seed.ts:397-404) instead of upserting each link?
items.back: An upsert can add a link but cannot express that a link is gone. Delete-then-insert for a small child collection is the simple correct way to make removals in content take effect.

items.prompt: Chapter 02 rejects modelling Reps's item kinds as a class hierarchy (McqItem extends Item). What problem does it name with that approach?
items.answer: Its instanceof checks stop working once a value goes through JSON.parse
distractors: Each subclass needs its own table, so every session load needs a join
TypeScript cannot narrow a subclass inside a switch on its kind field
Subclasses cannot share the prompt, explanation and level fields at all
items.explanation: Chapter 02 line 12: a class hierarchy is awkward to serialise to JSON, awkward to send across the server/client boundary, and needs instanceof checks that stop working once the value has been through JSON.parse. Table-per-kind is a separate storage alternative, and shared fields are exactly what a base class would provide.

items.prompt: Reps declares `ITEM_KINDS = [ ... ] as const` and `type ItemKind = (typeof ITEM_KINDS)[number]`. What does that single declaration provide?
items.answer: A runtime array to iterate and a compile-time type, from one source
distractors: A frozen array that throws at runtime if a new kind is ever pushed
A string enum the database applies as a CHECK on the kind column
A type only, erased at build time with no runtime value left over
items.explanation: Chapter 02 line 26: one declaration yields a runtime array and a compile-time type. The array exists so the app can iterate (ITEM_KIND_META: Record<ItemKind, ...> must have an entry for every kind or it fails to compile); the type exists so a switch can be exhaustive. Nothing here throws at runtime or constrains the database.

items.prompt: Response is a true discriminated union, but Grade is one type with optional detail fields plus required `correct` and `score`. Why does chapter 02 call that deliberate?
items.answer: Most consumers read only correct and score; details are per-kind extras
distractors: Grades are stored as JSON text, which cannot represent a union type
A union would force the grader to cast on every single return path
Grades arrive from the client, so their shape cannot be relied upon
items.explanation: Chapter 02 line 44: consumers mostly care about correct and score (ratingFor, the attempts table, the session summary), and the detail fields are only read by the feedback UI for the kind that produced them: put the fields every consumer needs in the required core and the per-variant fields in optional extras. Grades are computed by the server, not trusted from the client.

items.prompt: In Reps an Item with kind: "code" and an McqPayload type-checks, so the grader casts payloads. What actually keeps kind and payload matched?
items.answer: The DSL is the only producer, and check-content grades every item
distractors: toItem() runs a zod parse when it reads the payload from SQLite
The correlated ItemOf<K, P> union declared in src/types/index.ts
A CHECK constraint on the items table rejects mismatched payloads
items.explanation: Chapter 02 lines 60 and 70: kind and payload are not correlated in Item, so every `as` is a promise the compiler cannot check. It holds because the only producer of items is the DSL (blank() always pairs kind fill-blank with a FillBlankPayload) and scripts/check-content.ts grades every item against its own answer. ItemOf<K, P> is only a sketch (exercise 2), toItem() uses a plain JSON.parse, and SQLite will store any JSON.

items.prompt: An mcq-shaped response is sent to a fill-blank item. What does grade() do with it?
items.answer: It grades it as an empty answer, so wrong, and does not throw
distractors: It throws a TypeError, which the route then reports as a 400
It maps the chosen choice id onto the first blank and grades it
It returns null, and the route records no attempt for the item
items.explanation: Chapter 02 line 84: `response.kind === "fill-blank" ? response.values : {}` means an mcq response sent to a fill-blank item grades as an empty answer (wrong) and does not throw. That keeps the grader total, every input produces a Grade, which matters for a function the server runs on untrusted input.

items.prompt: grade(item, response): Grade has a case for all eight kinds and no default. What happens when someone adds a ninth kind to ITEM_KINDS?
items.answer: tsc reports a missing return in grade(), a to-do list for the kind
distractors: The new kind falls through at runtime and is graded as a wrong answer
check-content fails, because the new kind has no answer key to grade
ESLint flags the switch for lacking a default branch for unknown kinds
items.explanation: Chapter 02 line 88: because the return type is Grade and there is no default, adding a ninth kind makes TypeScript report that the function lacks an ending return statement; the compiler hands over the list (grade, emptyResponse, ITEM_KIND_META and every other exhaustive switch). A default would hide all of that, which is why the chapter says not to add one.

items.prompt: Reps stores each item's variant data in one JSON payload column that SQLite cannot validate. Why does chapter 02 say JSON wins here anyway?
items.answer: Payloads come from one trusted writer and are always read whole
distractors: Users author items in the app, so the shape has to stay flexible
SQLite lacks foreign keys, so per-kind tables would add nothing
JSON columns can be filtered as fast as normal indexed SQL columns
items.explanation: Chapter 02 line 107: JSON wins because payloads are written by exactly one trusted path (the seeder, from DSL-validated content) and read whole, never queried inside; the DSL assertions and the content linter replace the integrity the database gives up. If users could author items, or queries inside payloads were needed, the balance would tip the other way. The table credits per-kind tables with foreign keys and notes JSON cannot be queried efficiently.

items.prompt: Bug 5b: a retry test passed a function as input, and the first fix compared JSON.stringify of the round-tripped tests with JSON.stringify of the originals. Why could it never fire?
items.answer: Both sides drop the function identically, so the strings match
distractors: JSON.parse throws on null, so the check crashed before comparing
The tests lived in TypeScript, so the check never saw the data
Its comparison used ==, which treats null and a function as equal
items.explanation: Chapter 05 lines 53-60: both sides go through JSON.stringify, so both lose the function in exactly the same way; the comparison is '[null,3]' !== '[null,3]', which is always false, so the check looked like protection and gave none. JSON.parse handles null fine, and the comparison was a strict !== between strings.

items.prompt: What replaced the broken round-trip check for bug 5b, and what general lesson does chapter 05 draw from it?
items.answer: Walking the original values; make every new check fail on purpose
distractors: Storing tests as TypeScript; keep test data out of JSON entirely
A deep-equal of parsed values; compare objects instead of strings
A try/catch around stringify; let serialisation errors surface
items.explanation: Chapter 05 line 62: the real fix, findUnserialisable() in check-content.ts, inspects the original values before serialisation can hide anything and names the first value JSON would drop. Line 77: verify your verifier, because a check that cannot fail is worse than none, so feed a new check the exact bug and see it go red. JSON.stringify does not throw on functions, and parsed values have already lost them.

items.prompt: Bug 5c: a learner who answered every level-1 item correctly in one sitting still could not unlock level 2. Why, and what found the bug?
items.answer: Stability grows only across real days; an end-to-end script found it
distractors: Accuracy was counted per calendar day; a gate unit test found it
Coverage excluded second attempts; a learner reported it in the UI
Unlocking ran only after misses; the type checker flagged the branch
items.explanation: Chapter 05 lines 83-85: progression was gated on FSRS stability, which only grows when reviews happen across real elapsed time, so one perfect sitting gave modest stabilities. It was not found by unit tests (every function was individually correct) but by an end-to-end progression script that answered every level-1 item through POST /api/attempts and expected unlocked level 2.

items.prompt: Bug 5d: explanations with doubled or nested backticks rendered as garbled prose in the hand-written markdown renderer. What lasting fix did chapter 05 add?
items.answer: checkProse, a content lint that enforces the renderer's limits
distractors: A markdown library to replace the hand-written renderer for good
An escape pass inside renderMarkdown for doubled backtick runs
A visual snapshot test that renders every explanation in a page
items.explanation: Chapter 05 lines 112-114: the content was corrected and a permanent lint was added: checkProse() in scripts/check-content.ts fails on doubled backticks, an odd backtick count and nested backticks across every rendered string. The lesson: when you write your own parser, write the linter for its limits; the hand-rolled renderer and its single inline-code rule stay.

items.prompt: Bug 5h: the primer assertion in features.mjs passed on some runs and failed on others with no code change. What was wrong, and what was the fix?
items.answer: It hoped for an untouched module; now it finds one via /api/cheatsheet
distractors: It raced the server start; now it waits on a health check before running
It read Date.now() in render; now the timing ref is seeded in an effect
It shared port 3000 with dev; now the scripts start on their own port
items.explanation: Chapter 05 lines 153-155: the test sampled a mixed session and hoped it held a first-time module; on a well-drilled database it might not, so the result depended on the database's history. The fix constructs the precondition: ask /api/cheatsheet for every module, pick one with seenItems 0, and request a module-mode session for it, printing an honest skip if none is left.

items.prompt: In buildSession's default mixed mode, which items fill the session first, and up to how much of it?
items.answer: Overdue reviews, most overdue first, up to 60% of the size
distractors: New items from unlocked levels, easiest first, up to half
Low-accuracy cards from weak modules, up to one third of it
Seen but not-yet-due items, shuffled, up to 40% of the size
items.explanation: Chapter 06 lines 72-74: step 1 takes overdue reviews first, up to reviewBudget = Math.ceil(size * 0.6), most overdue first (sorted by due); step 2 fills with new items from unlocked levels; step 3 fills any gap with seen, not-yet-due items, shuffled. Spending the whole budget on reviews is weak mode, not mixed.

items.prompt: masteryScore() weights retention 0.7 and accuracy 0.3 and averages over every item in scope. Why does chapter 06 keep it apart from the level-unlock gate?
items.answer: They answer different questions: how durable versus how ready
distractors: Mastery is driven by accuracy alone, which a lucky guess inflates
The gate must use stability, while mastery must use plain coverage
Mastery is computed in the browser, while unlocking runs on servers
items.explanation: Chapter 06 lines 106-108: dividing by all items builds coverage into mastery, and mastery (a display metric driven by stability) is kept separate from unlocking (a gate driven by coverage and accuracy) because they answer different questions, how durable is what you know versus are you ready for the next material. Retention dominates mastery, and the gate deliberately avoids stability.

items.prompt: check-content.ts gives each check a negative case where possible ("a wrong answer fails") as well as a positive one. Why does chapter 07 insist on that?
items.answer: A grader that marks everything correct would pass positive-only checks
distractors: Negative cases let the linter run without loading the production grader
Warnings may only be printed once a failing example has been recorded
Negative cases stand in for the unit tests of every kind of question
items.explanation: Chapter 07 line 46: a grader that returned correct: true for everything would pass every positive-only check; the negative cases are what make the linter able to fail, the lesson of bug 5b applied systematically. The linter runs the production grader against each item's own key, and unit tests exist separately.

items.front: Item vs DrillItem, and why concepts are many-to-many (chapter 02)
items.back: Item is the domain object that gets graded and scheduled. DrillItem is a view model: the item plus everything the drill screen needs (track and module names, moduleKeyIdeas, concepts, isReview, reps), assembled in enrich() with batched inArray queries; the grader never depends on display fields. moduleKeyIdeas: null means the learner already touched the module, so no primer. item_concepts links items and concepts many-to-many: tracks organise content, concepts measure understanding.

items.front: FSRS in Reps: the model and its configuration
items.back: Each card has a stability (roughly the days until recall probability falls to the target) and a difficulty; ratings are Again 1, Hard 2, Good 3, Easy 4, and FSRS returns the next due date. src/lib/fsrs.ts sets request_retention 0.9 (higher means many more reviews for little extra retention, lower means forgetting more often) and enable_fuzz true (jitter so reviews don't clump on one day).

items.front: How Reps shapes the order of a session (interleaving, new modules, interview mode)
items.back: interleaveByTrack() picks the next item whose track differs from the previous one: blocked practice feels easier but retains worse, so interleaving is a desirable difficulty. spreadAcrossModules() sorts each module's new items easier-first, shuffles module order, then round-robins, so a new module opens gently. Interview mode draws from levels up to one above the unlocked one (capped at 4), round-robins tracks, and allows at most two items per module.

items.front: What in Reps's learning logic is research, and what is judgement?
items.back: Research supports the principles: spacing, retrieval practice, interleaving, pre-questions with scaffolds. It does not pick the constants: the 0.7/0.3 mastery weights, the 1.6x slow threshold, the 0.75 near-miss score and the 21-day mastery bar are tunable judgement calls. They are named constants or clear literals, so they can be tuned with data later; a senior engineer says which numbers are measured and which are guesses.

items.front: What `npm run check` runs in Reps, and in what order
items.back: typecheck (tsc --noEmit: shape errors and exhaustiveness) && lint (eslint src scripts, including the React 19 hooks rules; scripts/ is held to the same standard) && content:check (the domain linter) && test (vitest run, added to the chain on 2026-09-23). The chain is ordered cheap-to-expensive and stops at the first failure.

items.front: Reps's unit tests on arrival (Vitest, 2026-09-23) and the seams that make them possible
items.back: Four files under src/lib/__tests__/: grader.test.ts (every kind both ways, multi cancellation, normalizeBlank), executor.test.ts (the browser and node:vm runners incl. the hard timeout), utils.test.ts (deepEqual, renderMarkdown, date helpers, streakFromDays), fsrs.test.ts (ratingFor, a scheduling round trip). vitest.config.ts points REPS_DB_PATH at a path that does not exist, so a stray DB import fails loudly. Seams: streakFromDays(days, now) takes now; RunOptions.compile accepts a fake compiler that throws TimeoutError, a test double.

Bash heredocs silently mangled backslashes, so files were written with an editor tool. git had no identity, so it was set locally to match the existing author. CRLF warnings on every commit: understand core.autocrlf or add .gitattributes rather than ignoring them. Port 3000 was taken, and the process was identified before anything was done to it. Lesson: check the environment before acting on it.

items.front: Reps's API-level end-to-end layer: how it runs and why the API is the seam
items.back: The scripts drive the real HTTP API with fetch against a production build (npm run build && npm run start, not next dev) and assert on the JSON. scripts/e2e/e2e.mjs covers grading every kind both ways, FSRS behaviour, all session modes and server authority; features.mjs covers primers, the module and cheat-sheet endpoints and second-attempt credit; npm run e2e runs the scripts in order. The API layer is the right seam: it exercises route, grader, FSRS, session builder, Drizzle and SQLite together, and the JSON contract changes less often than markup.

items.prompt: Reps offers a second attempt after a first miss on mcq, predict-output and fill-blank items, but not on truefalse. Why does chapter 06 rule out a true/false retry?
items.answer: With the wrong pick gone, the retry would be a guaranteed win
distractors: True/false already earns partial credit, so a retry adds nothing
True/false items have their own iterate-until-correct loop instead
The server cannot cap a true/false score for a second attempt
items.explanation: RETRYABLE_KINDS (src/components/drill/Answers.tsx lines 37-42) holds mcq, predict-output and fill-blank. Chapter 06 line 66: multi, truefalse, order and code are deliberately not retryable, and a true/false retry is a free guaranteed win, because after one wrong pick the only option left is the right one, so nothing is retrieved. Partial credit is the reason given for multi and order, the iterate-until-green loop belongs to code items, and the server's second-attempt rule in POST /api/attempts does not look at the kind at all.
